newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai T-bill repo rates end down, spots mixed.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai T-bill repo rates end down, spots mixed.

text.p: Contracts on the treasury bill repurchase market in Shanghai closed down on Friday on heavy institutional selling late in the session, traders said.
Market sentiment was weakened on news Beijing had ordered the Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchange to come under the direct control of the central governement, traders said.
The annual rate for the most actively traded seven-day contract fell to 7.99 percent from 10.00 percent on Thursday.
Total turnover on the six-contract market soared to 4.08 million lots from 1.36 million lots on the heavy selling.
One lot is 1,000 yuan face value of treasury bills.
Contracts opened lower on the market centralisation news.

Fund demand for to a new domestic A share issue on Friday on the Shanghai stock exchange pushed up some early-maturing contracts before institutional selling in the final 30 minutes of trading forced all contracts to close lower.

Traders said the market centralisation would further check irregularities on the repo market after a series of crackdown meaures this year, including a ban on state banks trading on the exchange based state debt market.
"Market sentiment was weakened on the new measure, leading to the institutional selling," one trader said.

"The repo market is likely to continue to receive a negative effect from the news in the short term," he said. "But in the long run, the centralisation will contribute to standardisation of the financial markets."
Traders said they expected contracts to see a technical rebound on Monday following Friday's sharp losses.

Contracts on the T-bill spot market in Shanghai ended mixed, taking a break from rises in the past few days and with the new A share issue in Shanghai on Friday causing funds to flow out, traders said.
The most actively traded 10-year bond that matures in July 2006 fell slightly to 113.27 yuan from 113.29 yuan.
Combined volume on the eight-contract market fell to 1.04 million lots from 1.6 million lots.
Traders said some short-term investors pulled funds out of the spot market to bid for the new A shares, preventing contracts from rising again despite strong sentiment.
Traders said they expected the spot contracts to regain some ground early next week.
